quizzes.passage:
Farms That Grow Upwards

As cities grow and farmland becomes scarcer, some engineers and farmers are looking up rather than out. Vertical farms grow crops indoors, in stacked layers that can rise many metres high. Instead of sunlight, the plants receive light from LED lamps, and instead of soil, their roots often sit in water that contains carefully measured nutrients.

Supporters point to several advantages. Because the environment is fully controlled, crops can be harvested all year round regardless of the weather. Water is recycled within the system, so these farms typically use far less of it than traditional fields. Since insects are kept out, pesticides are rarely needed. And when a farm is built inside a city, vegetables can reach shops within hours rather than days, which reduces transport costs and keeps the food fresher.

Critics, however, are less enthusiastic. Lighting and climate control consume enormous amounts of electricity, and unless that energy comes from renewable sources, the environmental benefits may be smaller than they first appear. Building costs are also high, which is why most vertical farms focus on fast-growing, valuable crops such as lettuce and herbs. Staple foods like wheat or rice, which need a lot of space and time, are still far more practical to grow in open fields.

For now, then, vertical farming seems unlikely to replace traditional agriculture. A more realistic role may be to complement it, supplying cities with fresh greens while conventional farms continue to feed the world.
quizzes.text: Why can vertical farms harvest crops all year round?
options: Workers stay there day and night.
They use special seeds.
They are built in hot countries.
They grow only one plant.
The environment is fully controlled.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «The environment is fully controlled.».

quizzes.passage:
Farms That Grow Upwards

As cities grow and farmland becomes scarcer, some engineers and farmers are looking up rather than out. Vertical farms grow crops indoors, in stacked layers that can rise many metres high. Instead of sunlight, the plants receive light from LED lamps, and instead of soil, their roots often sit in water that contains carefully measured nutrients.

Supporters point to several advantages. Because the environment is fully controlled, crops can be harvested all year round regardless of the weather. Water is recycled within the system, so these farms typically use far less of it than traditional fields. Since insects are kept out, pesticides are rarely needed. And when a farm is built inside a city, vegetables can reach shops within hours rather than days, which reduces transport costs and keeps the food fresher.

Critics, however, are less enthusiastic. Lighting and climate control consume enormous amounts of electricity, and unless that energy comes from renewable sources, the environmental benefits may be smaller than they first appear. Building costs are also high, which is why most vertical farms focus on fast-growing, valuable crops such as lettuce and herbs. Staple foods like wheat or rice, which need a lot of space and time, are still far more practical to grow in open fields.

For now, then, vertical farming seems unlikely to replace traditional agriculture. A more realistic role may be to complement it, supplying cities with fresh greens while conventional farms continue to feed the world.

quizzes.passage:
In Defence of Boredom

We live in an age in which boredom has become almost impossible. The moment we have to wait — for a bus, in a queue, for a kettle to boil — most of us reach for our phones. It seems harmless: why sit doing nothing when there are messages to read and videos to watch? Yet a growing number of psychologists suggest that by eliminating boredom, we may be losing something valuable.

Boredom, they argue, is not simply an unpleasant emptiness. It is a signal that our current situation is not satisfying us, and it pushes us to look for something more meaningful. When the mind has nothing external to focus on, it begins to wander, connecting memories, ideas and plans in unexpected ways. Many people report that their best ideas arrive in the shower or on a long walk — precisely the moments when they are not being entertained.

This does not mean that every dull moment leads to brilliance. Chronic boredom, especially when people feel trapped in situations they cannot change, is linked to frustration and low mood. The difference seems to lie in how we respond. Boredom that we escape from instantly teaches us nothing; boredom that we tolerate for a while can become the starting point for curiosity and creativity.

Perhaps, then, the next time you are waiting for a bus, it is worth leaving the phone in your pocket. You may simply be bored for ten minutes — or you may have your next good idea.

as a signal that the current situation is not satisfying
as a sign of low intelligence
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «as a signal that the current situation is not satisfying».

quizzes.passage:
The Last Keeper

For thirty-two years, Ilyas had climbed the hundred and twelve steps of the lighthouse every evening to light the lamp. He knew every crack in the stone walls and every change in the sound of the sea. Ships passing the dangerous rocks below had never seen him, but many of their sailors owed him their lives.

The letter arrived on a grey morning in March. The lighthouse was to be automated: a computer in a city office would now control the lamp, and a keeper would no longer be needed. Ilyas read the letter twice, folded it carefully and placed it under the clock on the kitchen table, where it stayed for a week.

On his last evening, he climbed the steps more slowly than usual. At the top, he did not light the lamp; it lit itself at exactly the programmed minute. For a moment he felt useless, like an old tool left on a shelf. Then he noticed a small fishing boat struggling against the wind near the rocks. Out of habit, he picked up the radio and guided the fisherman to the safe channel, calmly, step by step, as he had done a hundred times before.

When the boat was safe, the fisherman's voice came through the radio: 'Thank you, whoever you are.' Ilyas smiled. Machines, he thought, could light a lamp. But they could not hear fear in a man's voice. He went down the steps for the last time, feeling, for the first time in weeks, that his work had mattered.

options: The lighthouse would be controlled by a computer.
The lighthouse would be closed and destroyed.
A storm was coming.
Ilyas would get a new assistant.
Ilyas had won an award.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «The lighthouse would be controlled by a computer.».

The Last Keeper

For thirty-two years, Ilyas had climbed the hundred and twelve steps of the lighthouse every evening to light the lamp. He knew every crack in the stone walls and every change in the sound of the sea. Ships passing the dangerous rocks below had never seen him, but many of their sailors owed him their lives.

The letter arrived on a grey morning in March. The lighthouse was to be automated: a computer in a city office would now control the lamp, and a keeper would no longer be needed. Ilyas read the letter twice, folded it carefully and placed it under the clock on the kitchen table, where it stayed for a week.

On his last evening, he climbed the steps more slowly than usual. At the top, he did not light the lamp; it lit itself at exactly the programmed minute. For a moment he felt useless, like an old tool left on a shelf. Then he noticed a small fishing boat struggling against the wind near the rocks. Out of habit, he picked up the radio and guided the fisherman to the safe channel, calmly, step by step, as he had done a hundred times before.

When the boat was safe, the fisherman's voice came through the radio: 'Thank you, whoever you are.' Ilyas smiled. Machines, he thought, could light a lamp. But they could not hear fear in a man's voice. He went down the steps for the last time, feeling, for the first time in weeks, that his work had mattered.

quizzes.passage:
The Paradox of Choice

It seems obvious that more choice is better. If a shop offers thirty kinds of jam rather than six, surely customers are more likely to find exactly what they want. Yet a well-known experiment conducted in a supermarket suggested the opposite. When shoppers were shown a large display of jams, more of them stopped to look, but far fewer actually bought anything than when the display was small.

Psychologists have proposed several explanations. Comparing many options demands time and mental effort, and when the differences between options are small, the effort can feel greater than the reward. Moreover, the more alternatives we reject, the more we may imagine that one of them would have been better, so even a good decision can leave us dissatisfied. Some researchers call this 'choice overload'.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that choice is simply harmful. Later attempts to repeat the jam study produced mixed results: in some situations a wide selection discouraged people, while in others it made no difference or even helped. The effect seems to depend on whether people already know what they prefer, how easy the options are to compare, and how much the decision matters to them.

The practical lesson, then, is not that we should eliminate choice but that we should organise it. Grouping options into clear categories, or deciding on our most important criteria before we start comparing, can turn an overwhelming decision into a manageable one.

options: Shoppers ignored both displays equally.
Small displays attracted more visitors.
A larger display attracted attention but led to fewer purchases.
Price mattered more than the number of jams.
A larger display led to more sales.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «A larger display attracted attention but led to fewer purchases.».

quizzes.passage:
Cities That Trap Heat

On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, is caused largely by the materials cities are built from. Asphalt, concrete and brick absorb heat from the sun during the day and release it slowly at night, so city centres often remain warm long after sunset.

The shape of cities contributes too. Tall buildings close together trap heat between them and block the wind that might otherwise carry it away. Air conditioners, cars and factories add further heat. Meanwhile, the trees and soil that would cool the land through shade and evaporation have often been replaced by hard surfaces.

The consequences are not merely uncomfortable. During heatwaves, higher night-time temperatures prevent the human body from recovering, which increases the risk to elderly people and those with heart or lung conditions. Higher temperatures also increase the demand for air conditioning, which in turn raises energy use and, unless the electricity comes from clean sources, adds to emissions — a vicious circle.

Cities are responding in various ways. Some are planting street trees and creating parks; others are painting roofs white so that they reflect sunlight rather than absorb it. 'Green roofs' covered with plants are becoming more common. None of these measures alone can solve the problem, but together they can make a measurable difference.
quizzes.text: What is the urban heat island effect?
options: Heat produced only by factories
Countryside temperatures rising faster than city temperatures
City centres being warmer than the surrounding countryside
Cities becoming colder at night
Islands being warmer than the mainland
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «City centres being warmer than the surrounding countryside».

quizzes.passage:
Remembering What Never Happened

We tend to think of memory as a recording: something happens, the brain stores it, and later we play it back. Decades of research suggest that this picture is misleading. Each time we recall an event, we partly rebuild it, and in the process details can be lost, changed or even added.

In a famous series of experiments, participants watched a film of a car accident and were then asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed into' or 'hit' each other. Those who heard the word 'smashed' gave higher speed estimates, and a week later they were more likely to report seeing broken glass — although there had been none in the film. A single word had quietly reshaped the memory.

Later studies went further, showing that some people could be led to 'remember' entire childhood events that had never taken place, such as being lost in a shopping centre, especially when the suggestion came from a trusted family member. Importantly, these false memories often felt just as vivid and certain as real ones.

These findings have serious implications for the legal system, which has traditionally placed great weight on the confident testimony of eyewitnesses. As a result, many police forces have changed how they interview witnesses, avoiding leading questions. The research does not mean that memory is worthless; most of what we remember is broadly accurate. It means that confidence alone is not proof of accuracy.
quizzes.text: Which view of memory does the writer challenge?
options: that memory works like a recording
that memory is studied by scientists
that memory can be changed
that memory is rebuilt when we recall
that some memories are false
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «that memory works like a recording».

We tend to think of memory as a recording: something happens, the brain stores it, and later we play it back. Decades of research suggest that this picture is misleading. Each time we recall an event, we partly rebuild it, and in the process details can be lost, changed or even added.

In a famous series of experiments, participants watched a film of a car accident and were then asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed into' or 'hit' each other. Those who heard the word 'smashed' gave higher speed estimates, and a week later they were more likely to report seeing broken glass — although there had been none in the film. A single word had quietly reshaped the memory.

Later studies went further, showing that some people could be led to 'remember' entire childhood events that had never taken place, such as being lost in a shopping centre, especially when the suggestion came from a trusted family member. Importantly, these false memories often felt just as vivid and certain as real ones.

These findings have serious implications for the legal system, which has traditionally placed great weight on the confident testimony of eyewitnesses. As a result, many police forces have changed how they interview witnesses, avoiding leading questions. The research does not mean that memory is worthless; most of what we remember is broadly accurate. It means that confidence alone is not proof of accuracy.
quizzes.text: Why is the broken glass significant?
options: It proved the cars were going very fast.
It showed the film was of poor quality.
It was mentioned in the question.
There was none in the film, so it was a false memory.
It was the cause of the accident.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «There was none in the film, so it was a false memory.».

quizzes.passage:
Whose Heritage?

Walk through the great museums of Europe and North America and you will see objects from every part of the world: sculptures, manuscripts, jewellery, religious items. Some were bought or exchanged fairly; others were taken during wars or colonial rule, often without the consent of the people who made or owned them. In recent years, demands for the return of such objects have grown louder.

Supporters of return, often called restitution, argue that these objects are not just works of art but parts of a community's identity and history. Keeping them abroad, they say, continues an injustice, and the communities they came from have the right to decide how they are displayed and interpreted.

Those who hesitate raise different concerns. Some museum directors argue that large international collections allow millions of visitors to compare cultures side by side. Others worry about whether objects will be stored safely, or point out that it is not always clear who the rightful owner is when borders and states have changed over centuries.

In practice, the debate is moving away from simple yes-or-no answers. Several museums have returned specific objects after careful research into their history, while others have agreed to long-term loans, shared research projects or joint exhibitions. What seems to be changing most is the starting question: no longer only 'Is this object legally ours?' but also 'How did it come to be here, and who has a stronger connection to it?'
quizzes.text: According to paragraph 1, how did museums obtain some objects?
options: Some were taken during wars or colonial rule without consent.
They were made by museum staff.
All were donated by their makers.
They were found in museum storerooms.
All were bought at fair prices.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Some were taken during wars or colonial rule without consent.».

quizzes.passage:
The Translator's Dilemma

When Kamala began translating a novel from Azerbaijani into English, she thought the hardest part would be the vocabulary. She was wrong. The hardest part was a single word that appeared on almost every page: the way the characters addressed one another.

In the original, an old woman calls the young hero 'bala', a word that literally means 'child' but carries warmth, protectiveness and a hint of authority all at once. 'Child' sounded cold and slightly insulting in English. 'Dear' was too sweet; 'son' suggested they were related, which they were not. Kamala tried leaving the word untranslated, but her editor worried that English readers would stumble over it and miss the emotion entirely.

For weeks she experimented. In the end she made a decision that some purists would criticise: she translated the word differently depending on the scene — sometimes 'my boy', sometimes 'dear one', occasionally leaving it out and showing the warmth through a gesture the old woman makes instead. 'A translator is not a dictionary,' she wrote in her introduction. 'My loyalty is not to each word but to what each moment makes the reader feel.'

Not every reviewer agreed. One complained that the variety 'flattened' a word the author had chosen deliberately to repeat. Kamala accepted the criticism calmly. Every translation, she said, involves losses; the question is only which losses you choose.
quizzes.text: What did Kamala expect to be the hardest part of the translation?
options: writing the introduction
the way characters addressed each other
the vocabulary
the length of the novel
working with her editor
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «the vocabulary».

quizzes.passage:
Treasure on the Ocean Floor

Thousands of metres below the surface of the Pacific Ocean, the seabed is scattered with potato-sized lumps called polymetallic nodules. They contain metals such as nickel, cobalt and manganese, which are used in the batteries of electric vehicles. As demand for these metals rises, several companies and governments are keen to begin mining the deep sea.

Supporters argue that deep-sea mining could reduce pressure on land-based mines, some of which have damaged forests and communities. They also claim that collecting nodules from the seabed involves less digging than traditional mining, and that the metals are essential for the shift away from fossil fuels.

Many marine scientists, however, urge caution. The deep sea is one of the least explored environments on Earth, and new species are discovered on almost every expedition. Some animals live on the nodules themselves, which take millions of years to form; once removed, these habitats would not return on any human timescale. Mining machines would also create clouds of sediment that could spread far beyond the mining area, with effects that are still poorly understood.

An international authority is responsible for regulating mining in waters outside national borders, and it has been debating rules for years. A number of countries have called for a pause until more research is done. The central difficulty is that we are being asked to weigh a known benefit against risks we cannot yet measure.

They are valuable as jewellery.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «They contain metals used in electric vehicle batteries.».

quizzes.passage:
The Clock Inside Us

Almost every cell in the human body contains a kind of clock. These internal timers run on a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours and influence when we feel alert or sleepy, when our body temperature rises and falls, and even when our digestive system is most active. Together, they produce what scientists call circadian rhythms, from the Latin for 'about a day'.

Because the internal cycle is not exactly twenty-four hours, it needs to be reset daily, and the most powerful signal for this is light. Morning light, in particular, helps keep the body's master clock, located in a small region of the brain, synchronised with the outside world. Without regular light cues, people's sleep patterns gradually drift.

Modern life often confuses these signals. Many people spend their days indoors under relatively dim light and their evenings in front of bright screens. Shift workers, who must sleep during the day, face even greater disruption. Studies have linked long-term circadian disruption to a range of health problems, although researchers stress that much remains to be understood about cause and effect.

Not everyone's clock runs at the same time. So-called 'larks' naturally wake early, while 'owls' feel most alert late in the evening. These differences are partly inherited and also change with age: teenagers tend to become owls, while older adults often drift towards becoming larks. Understanding this may lead to more flexible working and school hours that suit people's biology rather than fighting it.
